title: Networking and Content Delivery
intro: 18% of the exam, roughly 12 of the 65 questions. This domain is almost never 'design a VPC' — it is 'the packet did not arrive, tell me why'. Three mental models unlock it. First, the packet's checklist: for any connection, five things must all be true — route table entry, security group (stateful, both ends), network ACL (stateless, both directions), a public IP or a NAT path if the destination is the internet, and DNS resolving to the address you think it does. Second, statefulness is the diagnostic lever: because security groups auto-allow return traffic and NACLs do not, an ACCEPT on the inbound flow paired with a REJECT on the outbound flow can only be a NACL. Third, every symptom has an owning log — Flow Logs answer 'did the packet reach the ENI', ELB access logs answer 'who returned the 5xx, the load balancer or the target', CloudFront logs answer 'was it a cache miss or an origin failure'. Learn which log answers which question and half this domain becomes lookup rather than reasoning.

sections.title: VPC fundamentals as an operator
sections.summary: Addressing, routing, and internet egress: the four things that must line up before any packet leaves a subnet.

concepts.name: CIDR blocks, subnet sizing, and the 5 reserved IPs (plus IPAM)
concepts.explain:
A VPC CIDR is between /16 and /28 and cannot be changed after creation — you can only add secondary CIDR blocks (5 IPv4 blocks per VPC by default, raisable to 50). Subnet CIDRs are also /16 to /28 and cannot be resized at all; a too-small subnet is fixed by creating a new, larger subnet and migrating, never by editing.
AWS reserves 5 addresses in every subnet: the network address (.0), the VPC router (.1), the Amazon DNS resolver (.2, the VPC base + 2), one reserved for future use (.3), and the broadcast address (last). So a /24 gives 251 usable addresses and a /28 gives 11. That is the arithmetic behind the classic failure: an Auto Scaling group or an EKS node group stops launching, or a CloudFormation stack fails with 'InsufficientFreeAddressesInSubnet', because the subnet ran out of IPs — often because every pod, interface endpoint, NAT gateway, and RDS instance consumes an ENI address too.
Symptom: launch failures with InsufficientFreeAddressesInSubnet or an ASG stuck below desired capacity. Cause: subnet exhaustion. Check: the subnet's 'Available IPv4 addresses' count in the console, or the AvailableIpAddressCount attribute. Fix: add a secondary CIDR to the VPC, create larger subnets in it, add them to the ASG/subnet group. VPC IPAM is the org-scale answer: hierarchical address pools, allocation rules, and monitoring so accounts do not hand out overlapping CIDRs — which is what makes peering and Transit Gateway impossible later.
concepts.exam_tests: Any stem with 'instances fail to launch', 'stack rolled back with InsufficientFreeAddressesInSubnet', or 'the team needs more IPs in an existing VPC'. The discriminating fact: you cannot resize a VPC or subnet CIDR — you add a secondary CIDR block to the VPC and create new subnets. If the stem is about overlapping CIDRs across many accounts, the answer is IPAM.

example.scenario: An Auto Scaling group in a /28 private subnet keeps failing to scale past 6 instances even though max capacity is 20. The activity history shows InsufficientFreeAddressesInSubnet. Interface VPC endpoints and an RDS instance also live in the subnet.
example.answer: Associate an additional CIDR block with the VPC, create a larger subnet from it, and add that subnet to the Auto Scaling group.
example.why: A /28 has 16 addresses minus 5 reserved = 11 usable, and the endpoint ENIs plus RDS consume several. Subnet CIDRs are immutable, so 'modify the subnet to a /24' is not an available action; deleting and recreating the subnet would also require destroying everything in it.

concepts.name: Route tables, the internet gateway, and what actually makes a subnet public
concepts.explain:
Every route table has an undeletable local route covering the VPC CIDR — that is why instances in different subnets of the same VPC always reach each other regardless of route table (subject to SG/NACL). Route selection is longest-prefix-match: a 10.0.5.0/24 route to a peering connection beats a 10.0.0.0/16 route to a Transit Gateway, and the local route beats almost everything. A subnet with no explicit route table association silently uses the VPC's main route table, which is the single most common 'I created the route and it still does not work' cause.
A subnet is public only when its route table has 0.0.0.0/0 pointing at an internet gateway. That alone is not enough: the instance itself must have a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP. An instance in a public subnet with no public IP can receive nothing and initiate nothing to the internet. Auto-assign public IPv4 is a subnet attribute and is off by default on subnets you create.
Symptom: 'cannot SSH to my new instance' or 'the instance cannot reach the internet'. Check in this order: (1) route table associated with THAT subnet has 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-, (2) the instance has a public IP or EIP, (3) SG inbound allows the source and outbound allows the destination, (4) NACL allows both the request and the ephemeral-port return, (5) the IGW is actually attached to the VPC. Fix whichever is missing. Note that an EIP association changes the public IP but not the private IP, and a stopped/started instance loses an auto-assigned public IP.
concepts.exam_tests: Stems like 'an engineer created a route to the internet gateway but the instance still has no connectivity'. Discriminators: the subnet is associated with the main route table rather than the custom one, or the instance has no public IPv4 address. If the stem says the instance keeps changing address after a stop/start, the answer is an Elastic IP.

example.scenario: A CloudOps engineer launches an EC2 instance into a new subnet, adds 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxxx to a custom route table, and attaches a security group allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22. SSH from the office times out. The instance shows a private IP only.
example.answer: Assign an Elastic IP (or enable auto-assign public IPv4 and relaunch), and confirm the subnet is explicitly associated with the custom route table.
example.why: An IGW performs 1:1 NAT between a public address and the instance's private address; with no public address there is nothing to translate, so the packet never arrives. Adding more SG rules cannot fix a missing public IP, and a route table only takes effect on subnets explicitly associated with it.

concepts.name: NAT gateway vs NAT instance vs egress-only internet gateway
concepts.explain:
A public NAT gateway gives private-subnet instances outbound-only IPv4 internet access. Three placement rules are tested constantly: the NAT gateway lives in a PUBLIC subnet, it requires an Elastic IP, and the PRIVATE subnet's route table gets 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxxx. Putting the NAT gateway in the private subnet, or pointing the public subnet's default route at it, creates a routing loop or a black hole. A NAT gateway is zonal, not regional: if its AZ fails, private subnets in other AZs that route through it lose internet. Deploy one NAT gateway per AZ and point each AZ's private route table at its local NAT gateway — that also removes cross-AZ data transfer charges.
Capacity failures have their own signature. ErrorPortAllocation greater than zero means the NAT gateway could not allocate a source port — you have exceeded roughly 55,000 simultaneous connections to a single destination IP:port, usually a chatty poller hitting one endpoint. PacketsDropCount rising indicates the gateway is dropping traffic. The fixes are to spread load across more destination IPs, add NAT gateways, or remove the traffic from NAT entirely with a VPC endpoint.
A NAT instance is the legacy self-managed alternative. Its one uniquely tested fact: you must DISABLE the source/destination check on the ENI, because by default EC2 drops packets not addressed to the instance itself. It also needs a security group (a NAT gateway has none) and it does not scale or heal automatically.
An egress-only internet gateway is the IPv6 equivalent of a NAT gateway: stateful, outbound-only, no EIP, no charge for the gateway itself. IPv6 addresses are globally routable, so if you want outbound-only IPv6 you must use an EIGW with a ::/0 route — a NAT gateway does not handle IPv6 in that role.
concepts.exam_tests: Trigger phrases: 'instances in the private subnet cannot download patches', 'ErrorPortAllocation', 'must be highly available across AZs', 'IPv6 outbound only'. Discriminators: NAT gateway goes in the public subnet; NAT instance needs source/dest check disabled; IPv6 outbound-only means egress-only IGW; per-AZ NAT gateways for both HA and cross-AZ cost.

example.scenario: Private instances in three AZs route 0.0.0.0/0 to a single NAT gateway in AZ-a. During an AZ-a impairment, workloads in AZ-b and AZ-c also lose access to Amazon S3 and to a third-party API. The team also sees a growing NAT data-processing bill.
example.answer: Deploy a NAT gateway in each AZ, point each AZ's private route table at its local NAT gateway, and add a gateway VPC endpoint for S3.
example.why: A NAT gateway is an AZ-scoped resource, so one gateway is a single point of failure and forces cross-AZ traffic charges for the other two AZs. The S3 gateway endpoint removes S3 traffic from the NAT gateway entirely, which is free and cuts the per-GB processing charge.

concepts.name: VPC DNS attributes, DHCP option sets, and the .2 resolver
concepts.explain:
Two VPC attributes decide DNS behaviour. enableDnsSupport (default true) turns on the Amazon-provided resolver at VPC base + 2 (and 169.254.169.253); with it off, nothing in the VPC resolves anything through AWS, including private hosted zones and interface endpoint private DNS. enableDnsHostnames (default true only in the default VPC, false in VPCs you create) controls whether instances with public IPs get public DNS names. Both must be true for a private hosted zone to resolve inside the VPC and for interface endpoint private DNS to override the public service name.
A DHCP option set controls what the instance OS is handed: domain-name-servers, domain-name, ntp-servers, netbios settings. Pointing domain-name-servers at your own on-premises DNS servers replaces AmazonProvidedDNS — and that instantly breaks private hosted zones, interface endpoint private DNS, and EC2 internal hostnames unless those custom servers forward back to the VPC resolver. You cannot edit a DHCP option set; you create a new one and associate it, and instances pick it up on DHCP lease renewal (or reboot), not immediately.
Symptom: 'after a change, instances can reach IP addresses but no hostnames resolve'. Cause: DHCP option set replaced AmazonProvidedDNS, or enableDnsSupport was turned off. Check: the VPC's DNS attributes and the associated DHCP option set; from the instance, resolve against the base+2 address directly to isolate resolver vs configuration.
concepts.exam_tests: Appears as a prerequisite check inside private-hosted-zone and interface-endpoint questions: 'the private hosted zone does not resolve' → verify enableDnsSupport AND enableDnsHostnames. Also as 'after associating a custom DHCP option set, internal names stopped resolving'.

example.scenario: A team associates a custom DHCP option set pointing domain-name-servers at two on-premises DNS servers. Applications can still reach databases by IP, but calls to an interface VPC endpoint's private DNS name and to records in a private hosted zone now fail to resolve.
example.answer: Have the on-premises DNS servers conditionally forward the AWS-owned domains to the VPC resolver (base + 2) via a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint, or revert to AmazonProvidedDNS.
example.why: Replacing domain-name-servers removes the Amazon resolver from the instances' DNS path, and only the Amazon resolver knows private hosted zones and endpoint private DNS. Re-enabling DNS attributes alone does not help while the instances are still asking the wrong servers.

sections.title: Traffic filtering: security groups, NACLs, and the protection stack
sections.summary: Stateful vs stateless is the diagnostic axis; everything else is knowing which control sits at which layer.

concepts.name: Security groups vs network ACLs
concepts.explain:
A security group is attached to an ENI, is allow-only, and is STATEFUL: if you allow an inbound request, the response is automatically allowed out regardless of outbound rules, and vice versa. All rules across all SGs on the ENI are evaluated as a union — there is no order and no deny. SGs can reference other security groups, which is the correct pattern for tiering (the database SG allows port 5432 from sg-web, not from a CIDR), because it keeps working as instances scale and change IPs.
A network ACL is attached to a SUBNET, has both allow and deny rules, is numbered, and is STATELESS: return traffic must be explicitly permitted. Rules are evaluated in ascending number order and the FIRST match wins, so a broad allow at rule 100 makes a deny at rule 200 unreachable. The default NACL that ships with a VPC allows all inbound and outbound; a NACL you create yourself denies everything until you add rules — which is why 'the engineer created a new network ACL' followed by 'all traffic stopped' is a stock exam scenario.
Statelessness forces the ephemeral-port rule: whatever the client OS uses as its source port must be allowed back in. Because the client could be anything (Linux 32768-60999, Windows 49152-65535, ELB and NAT gateway 1024-65535), the tested convention is to allow 1024-65535 on the return direction.
Symptom and diagnosis: if traffic works in one direction only, or works for short-lived connections but not long ones, suspect the NACL. If a change to an SG had no effect, remember SGs are stateful — you probably did not need the outbound rule you added, and the real block is at the NACL or the route table.
concepts.exam_tests: Every 'the application can send but not receive' or 'traffic from the web tier to the database is blocked' stem. The discriminator is nearly always one of: NACL missing the ephemeral return range; a custom NACL denying by default; a lower-numbered NACL rule shadowing a later one; or an SG rule written with a CIDR where an SG reference was needed.

example.scenario: After a security team adds a custom network ACL to the application subnet, instances can still be reached on port 443 from the load balancer, but the instances themselves can no longer complete outbound HTTPS calls to a partner API even though the security group allows all outbound traffic.
example.answer: Add an inbound network ACL rule allowing TCP 1024-65535 from the partner API's address range (the ephemeral return traffic).
example.why: NACLs are stateless, so the outbound SYN is permitted but the inbound response arriving on a high-numbered ephemeral port is denied. The security group is irrelevant here because it is stateful and already tracks the outbound flow.

concepts.name: Layering order and the misconfigurations that produce it
concepts.explain:
Order matters when you are deciding where to fix something. For traffic entering a subnet: route table (is there a path at all?) → NACL inbound → security group inbound → instance/OS firewall. Leaving: security group outbound (stateful, usually already satisfied) → NACL outbound → route table. Network Firewall, when deployed, sits on a route between the subnet and its destination, so it is evaluated where the route sends the packet — which means a missing route to the firewall endpoint bypasses inspection entirely instead of blocking it.
The recurring misconfigurations are worth memorising as a list because the exam draws distractors from them: self-referencing SG missing (nodes in a cluster cannot talk to each other); SG allowing a CIDR that changed when instances scaled; a NACL numbered rule shadow; a NACL that allows the request but not the ephemeral return; a route table associated with the wrong subnet; a NAT gateway in the wrong subnet; an interface endpoint whose SG does not allow 443 from the client SG; and overlapping CIDRs making a peering route impossible.
Diagnostic shortcut: run VPC Reachability Analyzer between the source ENI and the destination. It analyses configuration statically and names the blocking component — SG, NACL, or route — without sending a packet, which also means it works when the instance is stopped or the application is down.
concepts.exam_tests: 'What should the engineer check FIRST' and 'which change resolves the issue with the LEAST effort'. The answer usually follows the layer order: verify the route and the stateless layer before adding more allow rules. Reachability Analyzer is the answer when the stem asks to identify the blocking component quickly.

example.scenario: An engineer must determine why an EC2 instance in a private subnet cannot reach an RDS instance in another subnet of the same VPC. The instance is currently stopped for a maintenance window and the team wants an answer before restarting it.
example.answer: Run VPC Reachability Analyzer from the instance's ENI to the RDS ENI and read the blocking component it reports.
example.why: Reachability Analyzer evaluates route tables, security groups, and NACLs statically, so it works without live traffic and pinpoints the exact rule. Flow Logs would show nothing because the instance is not sending packets.

concepts.name: Auditing the network protection stack: DNS Firewall, WAF, Shield, Network Firewall
concepts.explain:
These four are frequently confused because all of them 'block bad traffic'. They operate at different layers and produce different evidence, and the exam tests which one you inspect for a given symptom.
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall filters outbound DNS queries from your VPC against domain lists — it stops exfiltration and command-and-control by name, with actions ALLOW, ALERT, or BLOCK (block response NODATA, NXDOMAIN, or OVERRIDE). Evidence lives in Resolver query logs. AWS WAF is a layer-7 web ACL attached to CloudFront, an ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, or Cognito; it inspects HTTP requests with managed rule groups, rate-based rules, and custom rules, and WAF logs record the terminatingRuleId that blocked a request. Shield Standard is automatic and free for layer 3/4; Shield Advanced adds cost protection, the DDoS Response Team, and enhanced visibility on protected resources. AWS Network Firewall is a stateful VPC-level firewall (Suricata-compatible rules) deployed as endpoints in dedicated subnets with routes steering traffic through them — it handles non-HTTP traffic, domain filtering for outbound TLS SNI, and IPS.
Audit angle: a single-account review means checking, per VPC, whether a DNS Firewall rule group is associated, whether internet-facing ALBs and distributions have a web ACL, whether Shield Advanced protections cover the right resource ARNs, and whether the firewall subnet routes actually force traffic through the Network Firewall endpoints. AWS Config rules and Security Hub controls automate that audit; Firewall Manager is the multi-account version, though a single-account question expects the per-resource checks.
concepts.exam_tests: 'A request was blocked and users see 403 — how do you find which rule?' → WAF logs / sampled requests, terminatingRuleId. 'Prevent instances resolving known-malicious domains' → Resolver DNS Firewall. 'Filter non-HTTP outbound traffic between VPCs' → Network Firewall. 'DDoS cost protection and 24x7 response' → Shield Advanced.

example.scenario: Users of a CloudFront-fronted application intermittently receive HTTP 403 with a short generic body. The origin's ALB access logs show no corresponding requests at all for those attempts.
example.answer: Inspect the AWS WAF web ACL logs (or sampled requests) for the distribution and identify the terminatingRuleId that blocked the requests.
example.why: The requests never reached the origin, so the block happened at the edge — WAF or geo restriction, both of which return 403. WAF logs name the exact rule, which origin-side logs by definition cannot show.

sections.title: Private connectivity: endpoints, peering, Transit Gateway, VPN
sections.summary: Choosing and troubleshooting the private path between a VPC and AWS services, other VPCs, and on-premises.

concepts.name: Gateway endpoints vs interface endpoints vs PrivateLink endpoint services
concepts.explain:
A gateway endpoint exists for exactly two services — Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. It is not an ENI; it is a prefix-list route entry added to the route tables you select, it costs nothing, and access is governed by an endpoint policy. Because it is a route, it only works from inside the VPC: traffic arriving over VPN, Direct Connect, or a peering connection cannot use another VPC's gateway endpoint (no edge-to-edge routing).
An interface endpoint is an ENI with a private IP in each subnet you choose, powered by AWS PrivateLink. It has a security group (which must allow 443 from your clients — the single most common failure), it is charged hourly per endpoint per AZ plus per GB, and it CAN be reached from on-premises over Direct Connect or VPN. 'Enable private DNS' makes the public service hostname resolve to the endpoint's private IP inside the VPC, which requires enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames to be true.
A PrivateLink endpoint service is how you publish your own service to other VPCs: you put a Network Load Balancer (or Gateway Load Balancer) in front of your service, create an endpoint service, and consumers create interface endpoints to it. Connections are one-way from consumer to provider, require acceptance (or an allowed-principals list), and never need overlapping-CIDR-free address space — this is why PrivateLink is the answer when two organizations have conflicting CIDRs.
Symptom: 'the private instance cannot reach S3' — check whether the endpoint's route table is the one associated with THAT subnet, and whether the endpoint policy or the bucket policy denies (a bucket policy with aws:SourceVpce is a common cause). Symptom: 'the interface endpoint resolves but connections hang' — check the endpoint's security group.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Keep traffic to S3 off the internet with no additional cost' → gateway endpoint. 'On-premises servers must reach the service privately' → interface endpoint (gateway endpoints do not work from on-prem). 'Expose our SaaS to customer VPCs with overlapping CIDRs' → PrivateLink endpoint service behind an NLB.

example.scenario: Instances in a private subnet time out on s3:GetObject. The VPC has an S3 gateway endpoint and no NAT gateway. Another private subnet in the same VPC works fine.
example.answer: Associate the failing subnet's route table with the S3 gateway endpoint (add the endpoint's prefix-list route).
example.why: A gateway endpoint takes effect only in the route tables it is explicitly associated with; the working subnet uses a route table that has the prefix-list entry and the failing one does not. Adding a NAT gateway would fix connectivity but costs money and sends traffic over the internet path.

concepts.name: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway
concepts.explain:
Peering is a one-to-one, non-transitive connection. Three operational rules: CIDRs must not overlap, routes must be added on BOTH sides pointing at the peering connection, and there is no transitive routing — if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C. Peering also forbids edge-to-edge routing: you cannot use the peer VPC's internet gateway, NAT gateway, VPC endpoint, or VPN connection. Security group referencing across a peering connection works within the same Region; across Regions you must use CIDR-based rules. Peering has no hourly charge — only data transfer.
Transit Gateway is the hub. VPCs, VPN connections, Direct Connect gateways, and other Transit Gateways attach to it; TGW route tables control who can talk to whom via two independent operations: ASSOCIATION (which route table an attachment uses for its outbound lookups) and PROPAGATION (which route table learns that attachment's CIDRs). A missing propagation or a missing association is the standard 'the attachment exists but there is no route' failure, and it is separate from the VPC-side route table, which also needs a route to the TGW. A VPC attachment requires a subnet in each AZ you want reachable — traffic to an AZ with no attachment subnet is dropped. Inter-Region TGW peering requires static routes.
Symptom: 'peering traffic works one way'. Cause: the return route or the return-side security group/NACL is missing. Check both route tables and both SGs. Symptom: 'TGW attachment shows available but traffic is black-holed'. Check, in order: VPC route table has a route to tgw-, the attachment is associated with a TGW route table, the destination's CIDR is propagated into that table, and the attachment has a subnet in the source AZ.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Connect 30 VPCs with the least operational overhead' → Transit Gateway. 'Two VPCs need to communicate, minimum cost' → peering. Trap options rely on transitivity ('route through the peered VPC to reach the third VPC') and on forgetting the second-side route. TGW questions hinge on association vs propagation.

example.scenario: VPC-A is peered with VPC-B, and VPC-B has a NAT gateway. Instances in VPC-A cannot reach the internet through VPC-B's NAT gateway even though routes to VPC-B exist on both sides.
example.answer: Deploy a NAT gateway (or route through a Transit Gateway with a central egress VPC) for VPC-A; peering cannot provide edge-to-edge routing.
example.why: VPC peering explicitly does not allow a VPC to use the peer's internet gateway, NAT gateway, VPC endpoints, or VPN. Adding more routes cannot change that restriction; centralized egress requires Transit Gateway.

rows: Missing route on the return side

gotchas: Peering is non-transitive and has no edge-to-edge routing — no borrowing the peer's IGW, NAT, endpoints, or VPN.
Routes must be added in BOTH VPCs' route tables; a one-way route produces a one-way failure.
Cross-Region peering does not support security group referencing — use CIDRs.
TGW association and propagation are different settings; an attachment can be associated with a table that has no route to the destination.
A TGW VPC attachment needs a subnet in every AZ that must be reachable, and those subnets should be small dedicated ones.
The VPC route table still needs its own route to the TGW — the TGW route table alone is not enough.
Inter-Region TGW peering requires static routes; it does not propagate.
Appliance mode on a TGW attachment keeps a flow pinned to the same appliance AZ for stateful inspection.
numbers: TGW supports up to 5,000 attachments per gateway
TGW bandwidth up to 50 Gbps per VPC attachment

concepts.name: Site-to-Site VPN and Client VPN
concepts.explain:
A Site-to-Site VPN connection always has TWO tunnels to two different AWS endpoints, for AWS-side redundancy. It terminates on either a virtual private gateway (attached to one VPC) or a Transit Gateway (many VPCs). Routing is static or BGP; with a VGW you must either add static routes or enable ROUTE PROPAGATION on the VPC route table, and forgetting propagation is a stock failure. Each tunnel gives roughly 1.25 Gbps; more throughput means more connections with ECMP on a Transit Gateway.
Tunnel-down troubleshooting has a fixed order: check the CloudWatch metric TunnelState (0 = down, 1 = up) and TunnelDataIn/Out to see which tunnel; then verify the customer gateway's public IP is correct and reachable; then the pre-shared key and IKE/IPsec phase 1 and 2 parameters (encryption, DH group, lifetime) match on both sides; then that the on-premises firewall permits UDP 500, UDP 4500, and ESP; then that traffic is actually being generated — AWS does not initiate the tunnel, so with no interesting traffic and no DPD keepalive the tunnel can idle down.
Client VPN is the remote-user service: an endpoint with a client CIDR block that must not overlap the VPC, one or more target network associations (subnets), AUTHORIZATION RULES (which groups may reach which destination CIDR), and ROUTES. The two-part model is the tested trap: adding a route without an authorization rule, or vice versa, leaves users connected but unable to reach anything. Split-tunnel sends only VPC-destined traffic through the tunnel (cheaper, does not break the user's local internet); full tunnel sends everything, which is what you enable when you must inspect all user traffic.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Users connect to the Client VPN successfully but cannot reach the application' → missing authorization rule or route. 'One VPN tunnel is down' → this is expected/normal for redundancy unless both are down; check TunnelState and phase 1/2 parameters. 'On-premises can reach VPC-A but not VPC-B through the same VPN' → VGW is single-VPC; use Transit Gateway.

example.scenario: After creating a Site-to-Site VPN to a virtual private gateway with BGP, the tunnels show UP but instances in the private subnet cannot reach on-premises hosts. The private route table has only the local route and a NAT gateway default route.
example.answer: Enable route propagation from the virtual private gateway on the private subnet's route table (or add static routes to the on-premises CIDRs).
example.why: BGP advertises on-premises prefixes to the VGW, but they only appear in a VPC route table when propagation is enabled for that table. A healthy tunnel with no VPC-side route sends the traffic to the NAT gateway's default route instead.

Client VPN endpoint with subnet associations
Static routes or BGP + route propagation
Pre-shared key or certificate, IKE phase 1/2
Mutual certificate, Active Directory, or SAML/Identity Center
Route propagation on the VPC route table

gotchas: One tunnel down is a normal redundant state; the exam only calls it an incident when both are down or the workload fails over.
AWS does not initiate a VPN tunnel — configure DPD/keepalives or generate traffic from the on-premises side.
A virtual private gateway attaches to exactly one VPC; multi-VPC hybrid connectivity needs a Transit Gateway.
Route propagation is a per-route-table setting and is off by default.
Client VPN needs BOTH a route and an authorization rule for each destination CIDR.
The Client VPN client CIDR must not overlap the VPC or any routed network, and it cannot be changed after creation.
Split-tunnel disabled sends all user internet traffic through the VPC — you then need a NAT gateway and you pay for that traffic.
numbers: 2 tunnels per Site-to-Site VPN connection
~1.25 Gbps per tunnel
TunnelState metric: 1 = up, 0 = down
VPN uses UDP 500, UDP 4500, and ESP

concepts.name: Network cost levers
concepts.explain:
Cost optimization is an explicit task statement in this domain, and the exam tests it as a set of substitutions rather than as arithmetic. NAT gateway charges an hourly rate plus a per-GB processing fee on everything that passes through, so moving AWS-service traffic off the NAT gateway is the highest-leverage change: an S3 or DynamoDB gateway endpoint is free and eliminates both the processing fee and any cross-AZ hop. Interface endpoints are not free (hourly per AZ plus per GB), so they win on cost only when they displace a large NAT volume, and they are chosen mainly for the private path from on-premises.
Cross-AZ data transfer is charged in both directions. That is why a single central NAT gateway serving three AZs is a cost bug as well as an availability bug, and why cross-zone load balancing on an NLB (off by default) can add charges when you enable it. Traffic between instances in the same AZ using private IPs is free.
Egress to the internet is the other big line. Serving content through CloudFront costs less per GB than direct EC2/S3 egress and, with an origin shield or a high cache hit ratio, drastically reduces origin fetches. Origin-to-CloudFront data transfer out of AWS is free. For huge on-premises transfers, Direct Connect lowers the per-GB rate versus VPN over the internet.
Symptom: 'the NAT gateway bill grew without a traffic increase in the application'. Check: what is going through it. Fix: gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB, interface endpoints for the AWS APIs the fleet calls constantly (SSM, ECR, CloudWatch Logs), and per-AZ NAT gateways to kill cross-AZ charges.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Reduce data transfer costs with the LEAST change' → gateway endpoint for S3/DynamoDB (free) before anything else. 'Reduce cross-AZ charges' → per-AZ NAT gateways and AZ-local routing. 'Reduce internet egress for a media site' → CloudFront.

example.scenario: A data pipeline in private subnets writes several terabytes per day to Amazon S3 through a NAT gateway. Finance flags a large NAT data-processing charge on the bill.
example.answer: Create an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and add its prefix-list route to the private subnets' route tables.
example.why: A gateway endpoint carries no hourly or per-GB charge and removes the S3 traffic from the NAT gateway entirely. An interface endpoint would also work but adds hourly and per-GB charges for traffic that a gateway endpoint carries for free.

Only S3 and DynamoDB, only from inside the VPC
NAT gateway processing for AWS API calls
Interface endpoints for SSM, ECR, Logs, KMS
Hourly per AZ + per GB; worth it above moderate volume
Cross-AZ traffic to a central NAT gateway
One NAT gateway per AZ, AZ-local routes
More hourly charges, but removes cross-AZ per-GB both ways
Only helps cacheable or CloudFront-served traffic
VPN over the internet at high volume
Provisioning lead time and port charges

gotchas: Gateway endpoints are free; interface endpoints are not — do not answer 'interface endpoint' for an S3 cost question unless on-premises access is required.
Cross-AZ data transfer is charged in both directions, including between an ALB and targets in another AZ.
An idle Elastic IP not associated with a running instance still bills hourly.
Data transfer from an origin in AWS to CloudFront is free; CloudFront-to-viewer egress is cheaper than direct EC2 egress.
Enabling NLB cross-zone load balancing improves distribution but introduces cross-AZ data transfer charges.

sections.title: DNS operations with Route 53 and Resolver
sections.summary: Which record type, which routing policy, which health check, and how names resolve across VPC and on-premises boundaries.

concepts.name: Public vs private hosted zones and VPC associations
concepts.explain:
A public hosted zone answers queries from the internet for a registered domain. A private hosted zone answers only for the VPCs it is associated with, and it requires enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames to be true on every associated VPC. Split-horizon DNS is the normal pattern: the same domain name in both a public and a private zone, with the private zone winning inside the associated VPCs.
Associating a VPC from ANOTHER account is a two-step, API/CLI-only operation: the hosted zone owner runs create-vpc-association-authorization for that VPC ID, and then the VPC owner runs associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone. The console cannot do the cross-account flow, which is a favourite exam detail. Deleting the authorization afterwards does not break the existing association.
When a private hosted zone must serve many VPCs across accounts, the scalable pattern is a shared Route 53 Resolver rule set distributed by AWS RAM, or a central VPC with the zone associated to spoke VPCs.
Symptom: 'the private hosted zone record does not resolve from an instance'. Check: (1) both VPC DNS attributes true, (2) the VPC is associated with the zone, (3) the instance is using the Amazon resolver rather than a custom DHCP option set, (4) there is no overlapping zone (Route 53 uses the most specific matching zone). Symptom: 'resolves from the console/Route 53 test tool but not the instance' → the instance's DNS servers are wrong.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Instances in Account B must resolve names in a private hosted zone owned by Account A' → create-vpc-association-authorization then associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone via CLI/API. 'The private zone does not resolve' → check the two DNS attributes first.

example.scenario: Account A owns a private hosted zone for internal.example.com. Application servers in a VPC in Account B cannot resolve records in it. Both VPCs have DNS support and DNS hostnames enabled and there is no CIDR overlap.
example.answer: In Account A run create-vpc-association-authorization for Account B's VPC, then in Account B run associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone.
example.why: Cross-account association requires the zone owner to authorize the specific VPC and the VPC owner to complete the association; neither half works alone and the console does not offer this flow. Recreating the zone in Account B would duplicate records and drift.

rows: Delegated NS records at the registrar
Only via CloudWatch alarm-based health checks
Resolver query logs → CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Firehose

gotchas: Private hosted zones need BOTH VPC DNS attributes; this is the number one cause of 'it does not resolve'.
Cross-account VPC association is CLI/API only — the console path does not exist.
Route 53 health checkers are public, so a private hosted zone record pointing at a private IP cannot use an endpoint health check; use a CloudWatch alarm health check.
If the same name exists in a public and a private zone, associated VPCs get the private answer — non-associated clients get the public one.
The most specific matching private hosted zone wins when zones overlap (for example example.com and app.example.com).
Changing a domain's name servers at the registrar is required for a new public hosted zone; recreating a zone generates new NS records.

concepts.name: Alias vs CNAME, TTL, and propagation
concepts.explain:
An alias record is a Route 53 extension that maps a name directly to an AWS resource — ELB, CloudFront distribution, S3 website endpoint, API Gateway, Global Accelerator, VPC endpoint, or another record in the same hosted zone. Alias records can exist at the zone apex (example.com), are type A or AAAA, are not charged for queries, and automatically track the target's changing IP addresses. A CNAME maps a name to another name, is charged per query, and CANNOT exist at the zone apex — the DNS standard forbids a CNAME coexisting with the SOA and NS records that must live there.
That single fact answers a whole family of questions: 'point example.com at an ALB' is always an alias A record. 'Point www.example.com at a third-party SaaS hostname' is a CNAME, because alias only targets AWS resources.
Alias records also give you 'evaluate target health', which makes Route 53 consider the ELB or the aliased record's health without you creating a separate health check. Alias records to an ELB use the ELB's own TTL (60 seconds) and cannot be overridden.
TTL is the propagation lever. Resolvers cache for the TTL, so a cutover with a 3,600-second TTL takes up to an hour to converge for cached clients. Standard practice: lower the TTL to 60 seconds well in advance of the change, make the change, verify, then raise the TTL back. This is exactly the mechanism behind 'clients still connect to the old endpoint after an RDS Multi-AZ failover' — the endpoint name did not change, but a client or JVM cached the old address.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Users must reach the application at the apex domain' → alias. 'Reduce the impact of a planned DNS cutover' → lower TTL beforehand. 'After failover, some clients still hit the old IP' → DNS caching / TTL, not a Route 53 misconfiguration.

example.scenario: A team must point example.com (the apex) at a new Application Load Balancer. They created a CNAME record for example.com and Route 53 rejected it.
example.answer: Create an alias A record for example.com targeting the Application Load Balancer.
example.why: DNS does not permit a CNAME at the zone apex because the apex must hold SOA and NS records. An alias record is resolved inside Route 53 and returns the ALB's A records directly, so it is legal at the apex and free to query.

rows: AWS resources and same-zone records only
Inherited from the target (60 s for ELB)

gotchas: Alias targets must be AWS resources or another record in the SAME hosted zone — not an arbitrary external hostname.
You cannot set a custom TTL on an alias to an ELB; it uses the ELB's 60-second TTL.
An RDS Multi-AZ failover keeps the same endpoint name — client-side DNS caching, not Route 53, is why old connections persist.
Lower the TTL BEFORE the migration; lowering it at cutover time does nothing for already-cached answers.
Route 53 changes propagate to its own name servers within about 60 seconds, but downstream resolver caches obey the previous TTL.
S3 website endpoints support alias; S3 REST API endpoints do not serve a website — get the endpoint type right.
numbers: ELB alias TTL: 60 seconds
Route 53 change propagation to its name servers: typically under 60 seconds

concepts.name: Routing policies and health checks
concepts.explain:
Route 53 has eight routing policies and the exam picks between them on intent. Simple returns one record set. Weighted splits by ratio (weights 0-255; a weight of 0 removes a record, and all-zero weights makes them equally likely) and is the DNS-level canary/blue-green tool. Latency routes to the Region with the lowest measured latency for that client, which is NOT the same as geographic proximity. Failover is strictly primary/secondary and REQUIRES a health check on the primary. Geolocation routes by the client's country/continent/subdivision and needs a DEFAULT record or unmatched locations get no answer. Geoproximity routes by distance with a bias (-99 to +99) to expand or shrink a Region's pull. Multivalue answer returns up to 8 healthy records at random — a health-checked, cheap alternative to a load balancer, not a substitute for one. IP-based routing uses CIDR collections to map client networks to endpoints, which is how you steer specific ISPs.
Health checks come in three kinds. Endpoint health checks probe an IP or hostname from AWS's public checker fleet — so the endpoint must be publicly reachable; the default failure threshold is 3 consecutive failures, at a 30-second standard or 10-second fast interval. Calculated health checks combine up to 256 child checks with a threshold. CloudWatch alarm health checks derive health from any metric, and they are the ONLY way to health-check a private resource or a non-HTTP condition.
Symptom: 'failover did not happen'. Check: is there a health check on the primary at all, is the endpoint reachable from public checkers (SG/NACL must allow the Route 53 checker ranges), is the failure threshold and interval long enough that the outage was actually detected, and does the record use evaluate-target-health where relevant. Symptom: 'some users get no answer at all' with geolocation → the default record is missing.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Shift 10% of traffic to a new stack' → weighted. 'Send users to the lowest-latency Region' → latency, and the distractor is geolocation. 'Automatic DR to a static S3 site' → failover with a health check on primary. 'Health-check an instance in a private subnet' → CloudWatch alarm health check.

example.scenario: A failover routing configuration points the primary record at an ALB in eu-west-1 and the secondary at a static S3 website. During a Region impairment, users continued to receive the primary answer and saw errors. The primary record has no health check attached.
example.answer: Attach a Route 53 health check to the primary record (or enable evaluate target health on the alias) so failover can trigger.
example.why: Failover routing only moves traffic when Route 53 observes the primary as unhealthy; without a health check the primary is always considered healthy. Lowering the TTL would speed convergence but would never initiate the failover.

rows: Lowest measured network latency to a Region
Steering specific ISPs or corporate networks

gotchas: Failover without a health check on the primary never fails over.
Route 53 health checkers are public — a private endpoint can only be checked via a CloudWatch alarm health check.
Geolocation without a default record leaves unmatched users with no answer at all.
Latency routing is about measured network latency, not geographic distance; geolocation is the geography one.
Multivalue answer is not load balancing — no health-aware weighting, no connection draining, maximum 8 records.
Default failure threshold is 3; with a 30-second interval an outage takes roughly 90 seconds to be observed, plus TTL.
A weighted record with weight 0 receives no traffic unless every record in the set is 0.
numbers: Weights 0-255
Geoproximity bias -99 to +99
Multivalue returns up to 8 records
Health check interval 30 s standard / 10 s fast
Default failure threshold 3
Calculated health check: up to 256 child checks

concepts.name: Route 53 Resolver endpoints, DNS Firewall, and query logging
concepts.explain:
Hybrid DNS has exactly two directions and the exam always tests which endpoint you need. An INBOUND Resolver endpoint gives on-premises DNS servers IP addresses inside your VPC to forward to, so on-premises can resolve VPC private hosted zone names and EC2 internal names. An OUTBOUND Resolver endpoint plus forwarding rules sends queries from the VPC to on-premises resolvers, so instances can resolve corp.example.com. Both create ENIs in your subnets (two or more for HA) with security groups that must allow UDP and TCP 53. Forwarding rules can be shared across accounts with AWS RAM, which is how a central networking account serves an organization.
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall attaches rule groups to a VPC and filters outbound queries by domain list, with actions ALLOW, ALERT, or BLOCK, and a configurable block response (NODATA, NXDOMAIN, or an OVERRIDE record). Rule group priority determines evaluation order, and there is a setting for how to handle queries when the firewall fails.
Query logging splits by zone type. Public hosted zone query logging goes to CloudWatch Logs and is configured in us-east-1. Route 53 Resolver query logging captures queries from resources inside a VPC and can deliver to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Amazon Data Firehose — that is the log you read to prove an instance queried a malicious domain or to see what a DNS Firewall blocked.
Symptom: 'on-premises servers cannot resolve names in the VPC's private hosted zone'. Cause: no inbound endpoint, or on-premises is not forwarding the zone to it, or the endpoint SG blocks 53. Symptom: 'EC2 instances cannot resolve on-premises names'. Cause: no outbound endpoint or no forwarding rule associated with the VPC.
concepts.exam_tests: The direction test: 'on-prem → AWS names' = inbound endpoint; 'AWS → on-prem names' = outbound endpoint + forwarding rule. 'Which log shows the domain an instance queried' = Resolver query logs. 'Block instances from resolving known-bad domains' = Resolver DNS Firewall.

example.scenario: Applications on EC2 must resolve hostnames in the on-premises Active Directory domain corp.example.com, while on-premises monitoring must resolve records in a private hosted zone in the VPC.
example.answer: Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for corp.example.com to the on-premises DNS servers, and an inbound endpoint whose IPs the on-premises DNS servers forward the private zone to.
example.why: The two directions require two different endpoint types; neither one is bidirectional. Replacing the DHCP option set with the on-premises servers would break private hosted zone and endpoint DNS resolution inside the VPC.

Endpoint + Resolver forwarding rules associated to VPCs
Via the shared VPC / central account
Forwarding rules shared with AWS RAM
Security group does not allow TCP/UDP 53
Rule not associated with the VPC

gotchas: Inbound = into AWS. Outbound = out of AWS. Getting the direction backwards is the most common miss in this domain.
Resolver endpoints need at least two IP addresses in different AZs and a security group allowing TCP and UDP port 53.
Forwarding rules must be explicitly associated with each VPC that should use them.
Public hosted zone query logging goes only to CloudWatch Logs and is set up in us-east-1.
Resolver query logs (VPC-level) and public hosted zone query logs are different features answering different questions.
DNS Firewall evaluates rule groups by priority; a permissive high-priority group can shadow a block rule.
DNS Firewall does nothing against traffic that uses hardcoded IP addresses or a third-party resolver.

sections.title: Content delivery operations: CloudFront and Global Accelerator
sections.summary: Cache key and TTL decide hit ratio and staleness; status codes decide whether the fault is at the edge or the origin.

concepts.name: Distributions, cache policies, cache keys, TTLs, and invalidations
concepts.explain:
A distribution has one or more origins and a set of cache behaviours matched by path pattern (the default behaviour catches everything else, and more specific patterns are evaluated by precedence order). Each behaviour attaches a CACHE POLICY, which defines the cache key (which headers, cookies, and query strings are part of the identity of a cached object) plus the min/default/max TTLs, and an ORIGIN REQUEST POLICY, which defines what is FORWARDED to the origin without being part of the cache key. That split is the single highest-value idea here: forwarding a value the origin needs (like a User-Agent or an auth header) via the origin request policy costs you nothing in hit ratio, while putting it in the cache key fragments the cache.
Low cache hit ratio has a short cause list: too many values in the cache key (especially Cookie: * or all query strings), an origin sending Cache-Control: no-cache/no-store or a very short max-age, a min TTL of 0 with no origin caching headers, or genuinely unique per-user objects. Check the CloudFront cache statistics report and the CacheHitRate CloudWatch metric (additional metrics must be enabled). Fix by trimming the cache key, normalizing query strings, and setting sensible Cache-Control at the origin.
TTL arithmetic: if the origin sends Cache-Control max-age, CloudFront honours it but clamps it between the behaviour's minimum and maximum TTL. If the origin sends no caching header, the default TTL applies (24 hours out of the box).
Stale content has two fixes. Invalidation removes objects from edge caches now — the first 1,000 paths per month are free and further paths are charged, and a wildcard path counts as one path. Versioned object names (app.v37.js) are the preferred pattern because they never need invalidation and never race. Symptom: 'users still see the old file after a deploy' → either an invalidation was not issued or the browser cached it; check the object's TTL and the response headers.
concepts.exam_tests: 'The cache hit ratio is low' → look at the cache key (forwarded headers/cookies/query strings) and the origin's Cache-Control. 'Users see outdated content after a deployment' → invalidate, or better, use versioned file names. 'Forward a header to the origin without hurting caching' → origin request policy, not cache policy.

example.scenario: A CloudFront distribution serving mostly static assets shows a cache hit ratio near 10%. The cache behaviour forwards all cookies and all query strings to the origin, and the origin sets Cache-Control: max-age=86400.
example.answer: Attach a cache policy that includes only the query strings the content actually varies on and excludes cookies, keeping the needed values in an origin request policy if the origin requires them.
example.why: Every distinct cookie or query string combination creates a separate cache key, so a site with session cookies effectively caches per user. The origin's max-age is already generous, so the TTLs are not the problem.

Raises the floor even if the origin says no-cache
Applies when the origin sends no Cache-Control (24 h default)

gotchas: Cache policy = cache key. Origin request policy = what the origin receives. Confusing them is the classic hit-ratio trap.
Forwarding all cookies or Cookie: * is the fastest way to destroy a cache hit ratio.
Only the first 1,000 invalidation paths per month are free; a wildcard counts as one path.
Invalidation is not instant and does not clear browser caches — versioned object names avoid both problems.
Origin Cache-Control max-age is clamped between the behaviour's minimum and maximum TTL.
CacheHitRate and other per-distribution metrics require enabling additional CloudFront metrics (chargeable).
Path patterns are matched by precedence; a broad default behaviour placed above a specific one never lets the specific one run.
numbers: Default TTL 86,400 s (24 h); maximum TTL default 31,536,000 s (1 year); minimum TTL default 0
1,000 free invalidation paths per month
CloudFront origin connection timeout 10 s (default), origin response timeout 30 s (default)

concepts.name: CloudFront access control and error triage (403, 502, 504)
concepts.explain:
Access control at the edge has four independent mechanisms, and each of them returns its own status code, which is what makes triage possible. Origin access control (OAC, the replacement for the legacy OAI) lets CloudFront sign requests to a private S3 bucket; the bucket policy must allow the CloudFront service principal with an aws:SourceArn condition naming the distribution, and public access stays blocked. Signed URLs and signed cookies restrict individual objects (URLs) or whole path sets (cookies) using trusted key groups. Geo restriction allows or blocks by viewer country. Viewer protocol policy (redirect-to-HTTPS or https-only) and the origin protocol policy control the two TLS legs separately.
Triage table by symptom. HTTP 403 from CloudFront: OAC not configured or the bucket policy missing the CloudFront principal; a WAF rule blocking; geo restriction; an expired or malformed signed URL; or S3 returning AccessDenied because the object does not exist and the caller lacks s3:ListBucket (S3 returns 403 instead of 404 for a missing object when list permission is absent). HTTP 502 Bad Gateway: the origin returned something CloudFront could not parse — usually a TLS problem such as an expired or mismatched origin certificate, an unsupported cipher, or a Lambda@Edge function returning an invalid response. HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout: the origin did not answer in time — origin security group or NACL not permitting CloudFront, an overloaded origin, or an origin response timeout that is too short. HTTP 503 usually indicates capacity or too many requests.
Origin failover requires an origin GROUP with a primary and a secondary origin and an explicit list of failover status codes (such as 500, 502, 503, 504, 404, 403); it applies to GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS requests. Price classes (All, 200, 100) trade edge-location coverage for cost and change latency for distant users, not correctness.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Users receive 403 from CloudFront' → OAC/bucket policy, WAF, geo restriction, or signed URL. '502 from CloudFront' → origin TLS/certificate or Lambda@Edge response. '504' → origin unreachable or too slow; check the origin SG and timeouts. 'Serve private S3 content' → OAC plus a bucket policy, never a public bucket.

example.scenario: After migrating a distribution from an S3 website endpoint to a private S3 bucket with origin access control, all requests return 403 AccessDenied. The bucket has Block Public Access enabled and the distribution shows the OAC attached.
example.answer: Update the S3 bucket policy to allow s3:GetObject to the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal with an aws:SourceArn condition for the distribution ARN.
example.why: OAC makes CloudFront sign the request, but the bucket still denies it until the bucket policy grants the CloudFront service principal access. Disabling Block Public Access would technically serve the content but defeats the purpose and is never the intended answer.

OAC/bucket policy, WAF rule, geo restriction, expired signed URL, S3 missing object without ListBucket
WAF logs and the S3 bucket policy
Wrong origin path, missing object, wrong default root object
Origin path setting and the object key
Origin certificate expired/mismatched, unsupported cipher, invalid Lambda@Edge response
Origin domain certificate and origin protocol policy
Origin SG/NACL blocking CloudFront, origin overloaded, response timeout too short
Origin security group and origin response timeout

gotchas: OAC alone is not enough — the S3 bucket policy must grant the CloudFront service principal with aws:SourceArn.
S3 returns 403 (not 404) for a missing object when the caller lacks s3:ListBucket, which surfaces as a confusing CloudFront 403.
Geo restriction and a WAF block both produce 403; only the WAF log tells you which one acted.
502 points at the origin's TLS/certificate or an edge function response, not at CloudFront capacity.
504 is usually the origin's security group not permitting the CloudFront managed prefix list or the origin being too slow.
An ACM certificate for a CloudFront distribution must be issued in us-east-1, regardless of where the origin is.
Origin failover needs an origin group and a defined list of failover status codes; it does not trigger on timeouts alone unless the resulting code is listed.
Signed URLs cover one object; signed cookies cover multiple objects matching a path — do not swap them.
numbers: CloudFront viewer certificate must be in us-east-1
Origin response timeout default 30 s (1-60 s configurable)
Origin connection attempts default 3, connection timeout 10 s

concepts.name: Edge compute, CloudFront logging, and Global Accelerator
concepts.explain:
Two edge compute options. CloudFront Functions run only at viewer request and viewer response, in a lightweight JavaScript runtime with sub-millisecond execution, no network or filesystem access — use them for header manipulation, URL rewrites, simple redirects, and token validation at massive scale and very low cost. Lambda@Edge runs at four points (viewer request, origin request, origin response, viewer response), is authored in us-east-1 and replicated, can make network calls and access larger bodies, and is the choice when you need to call an origin or another service, do more than a few milliseconds of work, or generate content.
Logging. Standard access logs record every request delivered to S3 (and, with v2, to CloudWatch Logs or Data Firehose) with several-minute delay — this is the log you query in Athena for 'which URIs were 403 yesterday' or 'what is my byte volume by path'. Real-time logs stream a configurable sample of requests and fields to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams within seconds and cost more — use them when you need to react during an incident. The cache statistics report and the CloudWatch CacheHitRate metric answer hit-ratio questions.
Global Accelerator solves a different problem: it gives you two static anycast IP addresses, sends traffic onto the AWS backbone from the nearest edge, health-checks regional endpoints, and fails over across Regions in seconds without waiting for DNS TTLs. It supports TCP and UDP, so it works for gaming, VoIP, IoT, and any non-HTTP protocol, and it does not cache. CloudFront caches HTTP(S) content at the edge and is the answer for static and dynamic web delivery. If a stem says 'static IP addresses required', 'non-HTTP protocol', or 'fast Regional failover independent of DNS caching', it is Global Accelerator.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Rewrite a URL at the edge with the lowest cost and latency' → CloudFront Functions. 'Call an external API at the edge' → Lambda@Edge. 'Need two static IPs for a firewall allow-list' → Global Accelerator. 'Query all edge requests that returned 403 last week' → standard access logs in S3 queried with Athena.

example.scenario: A UDP-based multiplayer game runs in three Regions. Enterprise customers must allow-list a fixed set of IP addresses in their firewalls, and regional failover must complete in seconds without depending on client DNS caching.
example.answer: Put AWS Global Accelerator in front of the regional Network Load Balancers and publish its two static anycast IP addresses.
example.why: Global Accelerator supports UDP, provides static anycast IPs suitable for allow-listing, and shifts traffic on health-check failure at the network layer, so clients that cached DNS answers still fail over. CloudFront is HTTP(S)-only and does not provide static customer-facing IPs.

rows: TCP and UDP, any application protocol
Origin group failover on listed status codes
Traffic dials per Region and endpoint weights
Static and dynamic web content, media
Non-HTTP workloads, static IP requirements, fast Regional failover

gotchas: CloudFront Functions cannot make network calls and only run at viewer request/response — anything origin-side needs Lambda@Edge.
Lambda@Edge functions must be created in us-east-1 and published as a numbered version; $LATEST cannot be associated.
Standard access logs are delayed by minutes; real-time logs go to Kinesis Data Streams and are the incident-time tool.
Global Accelerator does not cache — pairing it with CloudFront is for different problems, not a substitute.
Price class changes which edge locations serve traffic; it affects latency and cost, never correctness.
CloudFront metrics beyond the basic set (including CacheHitRate) require enabling additional metrics.

sections.title: The troubleshooting toolkit and canonical flows
sections.summary: Which log or analyzer answers which question, and the five connectivity failures the exam recycles.

concepts.name: VPC Flow Logs: fields, statuses, and the SG-vs-NACL diagnosis
concepts.explain:
Flow Logs capture IP flow METADATA — not packet contents — at the VPC, subnet, or ENI level, delivered to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Amazon Data Firehose. The default record is: version, account-id, interface-id, srcaddr, dstaddr, srcport, dstport, protocol, packets, bytes, start, end, action, log-status. You can pick custom fields (including pkt-srcaddr, pkt-dstaddr, tcp-flags, flow-direction, traffic-path) but only at creation — a flow log cannot be edited, so a change means delete and recreate.
The action field is ACCEPT or REJECT and reflects the combined SG + NACL decision for that direction. log-status is OK (data delivered), NODATA (no traffic in the window), or SKIPDATA (records were dropped due to an internal capacity constraint) — NODATA and SKIPDATA are about the logging pipeline, not about the traffic being blocked, and the exam uses that distinction.
The headline diagnostic: because security groups are stateful, if the request direction shows ACCEPT and the response direction shows REJECT, a security group cannot be responsible (it would have allowed the return automatically) — so the culprit is a network ACL. If the request direction itself shows REJECT, it could be either an SG or a NACL. And if there is no record at all for the destination ENI, the packet never got there: suspect routing.
For volume, ship flow logs to S3 in Parquet with hourly partitions and query with Athena; the exam favours 'S3 + Athena' for retrospective analysis and CloudWatch Logs Insights for smaller, near-real-time investigations.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Flow logs show ACCEPT inbound and REJECT outbound' → NACL. 'Flow logs show no entries' → routing or the wrong capture point. 'log-status NODATA' → no traffic, not a block. 'Analyze months of flow logs cheaply' → S3 + Athena.

example.scenario: An application server cannot complete requests to a partner service. VPC Flow Logs for the instance ENI show ACCEPT on the outbound flow to the partner IP and REJECT on the corresponding inbound flow from that IP.
example.answer: Add an inbound network ACL rule permitting the ephemeral port range 1024-65535 from the partner's address range.
example.why: A security group would have allowed the return traffic automatically because it is stateful, so an inbound REJECT on a flow whose outbound half was ACCEPTed can only come from the stateless network ACL. Modifying the security group would change nothing.

rows: Inbound ACCEPT, outbound REJECT (or vice versa)
Add the ephemeral/return rule to the NACL
REJECT on the initiating direction only
Security group or NACL inbound rule missing
Add the SG rule (prefer an SG reference); check NACL
No records at all at the destination ENI
Check route table association, TGW/peering routes, blackhole routes
ACCEPT both directions but the app fails
Network is fine; application or TLS layer
Check the service, port, and certificates
No traffic in that aggregation window
Nothing to fix in the network; confirm the client is sending
Records dropped by the logging pipeline
Reduce scope or accept gaps; do not read as a block

gotchas: Flow logs record metadata, not payloads — for packet contents you need Traffic Mirroring.
You cannot modify a flow log's fields, filter, or aggregation interval after creation; delete and recreate.
Flow logs do not capture traffic to the Amazon DNS server, instance metadata (169.254.169.254), Amazon Time Sync, DHCP, or Windows license activation.
A REJECT record does not name the rule that blocked it — use Reachability Analyzer for that.
Default aggregation interval is 10 minutes; 1 minute is available and shortens detection time.
Enabling flow logs at the VPC level covers every ENI including ones created later — subnet or ENI scope does not.
numbers: Aggregation interval: 10 minutes (default) or 1 minute
log-status values: OK, NODATA, SKIPDATA
Destinations: CloudWatch Logs, S3, Amazon Data Firehose

concepts.name: Which log answers which question: ELB, WAF, CloudFront, container logs
concepts.explain:
The exam repeatedly asks you to choose a log rather than to read one, so memorize the mapping.
ELB access logs (S3, delivered every 5 minutes by default) contain both elb_status_code and target_status_code. That pair is the whole diagnosis: an elb_status_code of 502/503/504 with a blank or '-' target_status_code means the load balancer generated the error itself (no healthy targets, target reset the connection, target did not answer within the 60-second idle timeout). A matching pair means the target genuinely returned that code and the application is at fault. The timing fields request_processing_time, target_processing_time, and response_processing_time isolate where latency lives, and a -1 means that phase never completed.
WAF logs record every inspected request with the terminatingRuleId, so they answer 'which rule blocked this user'. CloudFront standard access logs record x-edge-result-type (Hit, Miss, RefreshHit, Error, LimitExceeded), which answers cache questions and edge error questions that origin logs cannot see. Container logs: ECS tasks use the awslogs log driver (awslogs-group, awslogs-region, awslogs-stream-prefix) and the task EXECUTION role needs CloudWatch Logs permissions — missing that permission is why a task starts and produces no logs; EKS control-plane logs (api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, scheduler) are opt-in per cluster and go to CloudWatch Logs, and they are how you investigate authentication and admission failures that pod logs never show.
Symptom-to-log: 'users get 503' → ELB access logs plus target group health. 'requests never reach the origin' → WAF and CloudFront logs. 'the container starts and dies silently' → the awslogs stream, or the task execution role if the stream is missing entirely.
concepts.exam_tests: 'Which log should the engineer analyze?' is a whole question family. Discriminators: ELB access logs for elb vs target status codes; WAF logs for the blocking rule; CloudFront logs for edge result type; Resolver query logs for DNS; Flow Logs for allow/deny at the network layer; CloudTrail for who made an API call.

example.scenario: Users intermittently receive HTTP 504 from an Application Load Balancer. The engineer must determine whether the load balancer or the application is producing the error.
example.answer: Enable and analyze ALB access logs, comparing elb_status_code with target_status_code and target_processing_time.
example.why: A 504 with an empty target_status_code and a target_processing_time at the idle timeout proves the target failed to respond in time, whereas matching codes would prove the application returned the 504 itself. CloudWatch metrics show the count but not the per-request attribution.

rows: Was the packet allowed onto the ENI?
Did the ALB or the app produce the 5xx?
Was it a cache hit or an origin error?
What domain did the instance resolve?
Why did the container produce nothing?
Task execution role permissions, stopped reason
Why was the kubectl call denied?

gotchas: ALB access logs are off by default and require an S3 bucket policy allowing the log delivery service.
A '-' or blank target_status_code with a 5xx elb_status_code means the load balancer produced the error, not the app.
A processing-time field of -1 means that phase never completed (usually the target never responded).
ECS tasks with no logs at all are usually missing CloudWatch Logs permissions on the task EXECUTION role, not the task role.
EKS control-plane logging is disabled by default and must be enabled per log type on the cluster.
CloudFront logs and ALB logs both exist for a CloudFront-in-front-of-ALB stack; only the CloudFront log sees requests blocked at the edge.
CloudTrail answers 'who changed it', never 'was the packet dropped'.
numbers: ALB access log delivery interval: 5 minutes (default) or 60 minutes
ALB idle timeout default 60 seconds
EKS control-plane log types: api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, scheduler

concepts.name: Analyzers and network monitoring: Reachability Analyzer, Network Access Analyzer, Network Monitor, Internet Monitor, Traffic Mirroring
concepts.explain:
These five tools answer questions logs cannot. VPC Reachability Analyzer performs static configuration analysis between a source and a destination ENI/gateway and tells you whether a path exists and, if not, WHICH component blocks it — route table, security group, or NACL. It sends no packets, so it works against stopped instances and does not depend on the application. Network Access Analyzer works in the opposite direction: you define scopes describing unintended access (for example 'any path from the internet to a database subnet') and it finds every path that matches, across accounts — an audit tool, not an incident tool.
CloudWatch Network Monitor creates managed probes between your VPC subnets and on-premises destinations and reports packet loss and round-trip time, which is how you prove whether a hybrid problem is on the AWS side or the network provider's. CloudWatch Internet Monitor watches internet health between your users' city-networks (ISP + geography) and your AWS-hosted application, surfacing availability and performance events caused by ISPs or internet paths — the answer for 'users in one country report slowness but our metrics are clean'.
Traffic Mirroring copies actual packets from a source ENI (on Nitro instances) to a target ENI, NLB, or GWLB for deep inspection by an IDS. It is the only option when the requirement is packet-level content, since Flow Logs are metadata only.
Symptom-to-tool: 'identify the blocking rule fast' → Reachability Analyzer. 'prove no internet path exists to the data subnet' → Network Access Analyzer. 'is the VPN path lossy' → Network Monitor. 'is the internet degraded for our users' → Internet Monitor. 'capture the payload for the IDS' → Traffic Mirroring.
concepts.exam_tests: Distractors mix these deliberately. Key discriminators: Reachability Analyzer = one path, names the blocking component, no packets. Network Access Analyzer = compliance sweep for unintended paths. Internet Monitor = viewer-side internet health. Network Monitor = hybrid/VPC probe metrics. Traffic Mirroring = actual packets.

example.scenario: A security review must prove that no network path exists from the internet to any subnet containing database instances, across all VPCs in the account, and must be repeatable.
example.answer: Use Network Access Analyzer with a scope describing internet-to-database-subnet paths and review the findings.
example.why: Network Access Analyzer evaluates all possible paths against a declared scope and is designed for repeatable audits. Reachability Analyzer would have to be run manually for every source and destination pair and answers only one path per run.

rows: Can A reach B, and what blocks it?
Is the hybrid/VPC path lossy or slow?
Is the internet degraded for our users?
What is actually in the packets?
Source ENI to a mirror target

gotchas: Reachability Analyzer will report a reachable path even when the application is down — it checks configuration, not service health.
Traffic Mirroring requires Nitro-based instances and consumes source instance bandwidth.
Internet Monitor is about the viewer side of the internet; it does not diagnose anything inside your VPC.
Network Access Analyzer is an audit sweep; do not pick it for a live 'why is this connection failing' incident.
Flow Logs cannot show packet contents — if the requirement says payload or deep packet inspection, it is Traffic Mirroring.

concepts.name: The five canonical connectivity flows
concepts.explain:
The exam recycles the same five failures. Learn the ordered check for each and you can answer them without reasoning from scratch.
1) 'Instance cannot reach the internet.' Check: route 0.0.0.0/0 → igw- for a public subnet or → nat- for a private one; the route table is actually ASSOCIATED with that subnet; the instance has a public IP/EIP (public subnet only); the NAT gateway is in a public subnet with an EIP and its own route to the IGW; SG outbound; NACL both directions including ephemeral return.
2) 'Private instance cannot reach S3.' Check: gateway endpoint exists AND its prefix-list route is in the route table associated with that subnet; the endpoint policy allows the action; the bucket policy does not deny via aws:SourceVpce/aws:SourceVpc; the bucket is in the same Region as the gateway endpoint. Fall back to a NAT gateway only if the bucket is in another Region or on-premises access is needed.
3) 'Peering traffic works one way.' Check: routes on BOTH sides pointing at the pcx-; SG rules on the responding side (remember cross-Region peering cannot reference security groups); NACLs on both subnets; no CIDR overlap; and remember peering is non-transitive with no edge-to-edge routing.
4) 'On-premises cannot resolve VPC names.' Check: a Route 53 Resolver INBOUND endpoint exists with IPs in two AZs; the on-premises DNS has a conditional forwarder for the zone pointing at those IPs; the endpoint's security group allows TCP and UDP 53 from the on-premises CIDR; the private hosted zone is associated with the VPC and both VPC DNS attributes are true.
5) 'TGW attachment exists but there is no route.' Check, in order: the VPC route table has a route to tgw-; the attachment is ASSOCIATED with a TGW route table; the destination CIDR is PROPAGATED (or statically added) into that table; the attachment has a subnet in the source AZ; the destination side has a symmetric return route; and for inter-Region peering, static routes are configured.
concepts.exam_tests: These appear as 'what should the engineer check FIRST' or 'which two actions resolve the issue (Choose two.)'. The most common single missing item across all five: the route table is not associated with the subnet in question, or the return path is missing.

example.scenario: Instances in a private subnet can reach an S3 bucket in the same Region but cannot reach an S3 bucket in another Region. The VPC has an S3 gateway endpoint and no NAT gateway.
example.answer: Add a NAT gateway (or a cross-Region-capable path such as an interface endpoint plus routing) because a gateway endpoint only serves buckets in the same Region.
example.why: Gateway endpoints are Regional: the prefix list contains only the local Region's S3 address ranges, so cross-Region requests have no route. Adding a second gateway endpoint is not possible for another Region's S3 service.

rows: Route table not associated, or no public IP
Gateway endpoint route in that subnet's table
Endpoint not associated with the route table
SGs and NACLs on the responding side
Missing return route or return SG rule
On-prem conditional forwarder and endpoint SG port 53
No inbound endpoint, or SG blocking 53
VPC route table route to tgw-
TGW route table association and propagation
Propagation not enabled for that route table

gotchas: In every one of these five, verify the route table ASSOCIATION, not just the presence of the route.
Return paths are half the answer: peering, TGW, and VPN all need symmetric routes.
Gateway endpoints are same-Region only and do not serve on-premises or peered VPCs.
'Cannot resolve' and 'cannot connect' are different failures — test with dig/nslookup before touching security groups.
For TGW, association (which table the attachment uses) and propagation (which table learns its routes) fail independently.
A blackhole route in a route table means the target no longer exists — delete and recreate the route after replacing a NAT gateway or gateway.

end_of_domain_checklist: I can compute usable IPs in a subnet and explain why 5 addresses are reserved.
I can say why a VPC or subnet CIDR cannot be resized and what you do instead.
I can place a NAT gateway correctly and name the metric that proves port exhaustion.
I can explain when an egress-only internet gateway is required instead of a NAT gateway.
I can state the two VPC DNS attributes and everything that breaks when they are off.
I can diagnose a NACL problem from a Flow Log pair without looking at any rule.
I can say why adding an outbound security group rule rarely fixes anything.
I can say why a gateway endpoint is free, Region-scoped, and useless from on-premises.
I can name the one thing that makes an interface endpoint hang after DNS resolves correctly.
I can explain why peering cannot borrow the peer's NAT gateway or internet gateway.
I can distinguish a Transit Gateway association failure from a propagation failure.
I can list the tunnel-down check order for a Site-to-Site VPN and the metric to read.
I can name the two things a Client VPN needs for every destination CIDR.
I can pick alias vs CNAME instantly and say why the apex forces the choice.
I can choose among the eight routing policies and name which one requires a health check.
I can health-check a private endpoint and explain why an endpoint health check cannot.
I can pick inbound vs outbound Resolver endpoint from the direction in the stem.
I can raise a CloudFront cache hit ratio by moving values from the cache policy to the origin request policy.
I can triage a CloudFront 403, 502, and 504 to the right layer in one step.
I can pick Global Accelerator over CloudFront from a single phrase in the stem.
I can name the log that answers each of: allowed or denied, ALB or app, which WAF rule, cache hit or miss, which domain was queried.
I can choose between Reachability Analyzer, Network Access Analyzer, Internet Monitor, and Traffic Mirroring for a given symptom.
